claims.text: Uniformly dispersed nanoscale refractory particles will improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of high-entropy alloys.
Mechanical alloying followed by tailored heat treatments can introduce a uniform dispersion of nanoscale Y2O3 or TiC particles into the alloy matrix.
The dispersed refractory particles will act as obstacles at grain boundaries.
The dispersed refractory particles will obstruct dislocation motion.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by refractory particles will increase high-temperature tensile strength.
The refractory particles will hinder grain-boundary sliding at high temperatures.
Hindering grain-boundary sliding will enhance creep resistance.
The refractory-particle dispersion will stabilize the microstructure against grain coarsening.
Relative to an otherwise comparable unreinforced equiatomic high-entropy alloy, the reinforced alloy will have significantly greater tensile strength above 700°C.
Relative to an otherwise comparable unreinforced equiatomic high-entropy alloy, the reinforced alloy will have a lower creep rate above 700°C.
The predicted benefits should hold under sustained exposure from 700°C to 1000°C and moderate mechanical loading.
The predicted benefits may not persist during extreme thermal cycling or at stresses far outside the tested regime.
The optimal particle type, concentration, and dispersion method for this intervention are uncertain.
There is a current lack of direct experimental evidence for the proposed intervention in the specified high-entropy-alloy systems.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome identifies a lower creep rate as an improvement, but the falsification rule says the hypothesis is falsified when reinforced samples 'demonstrate lower creep rates' alongside no significant tensile-strength improvement. A lower creep rate is supportive rather than falsifying evidence; the rule likely intended to say that the samples do not demonstrate lower creep rates.
